newsitem.title: ISRAEL: France says Jerusalem issue won't harm Israel ties.
newsitem.headline: France says Jerusalem issue won't harm Israel ties.

text.p: French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said on Tuesday Israel's plan to build a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem would not harm its ties with France.

"Between friends -- I would even say intimate friends -- there are of course disputes on some subjects. But these disputes do not cause a conflict," de Charette told reporters after holding talks with Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy in Jerusalem.

France has lent its voice to a growing chorus of worldwide criticism of Israel's decision last week to build 6,500 homes for Jews in East Jerusalem, where Palestinians hope to build the capital of a future state.
But de Charette refrained from criticising Israel in a bid to mend ties with the Jewish state which hit a low during a rancorous state visit by French President Jacques Chirac last October.
Chirac irked Israelis but cheered Palestinians when he locked horns with Israeli police while touring Jerusalem's Old City and openly called for the establishment of a Palestinian state.
Israel captured East Jerusalem in 1967 and later annexed it in a move not recognised internationally.
France and Israel agreed to set up a high-level joint committee to coordinate and stabilise ties in all fields. "It is possible to say that our relations have taken a step up," Levy said.

Only last week, the Israeli Foreign Ministry lodged a complaint with the French ambassador after France announced de Charette would spend only 24 hours in Israel. The ministry said France had promised "a full state visit of two or three days".

De Charette was in Israel as part of a three-day regional visit aimed at boosting France's regional influence and to try to give a shove to stalled peace moves between Israel and arch-foe Syria. He will also travel to Lebanon and Damascus.
Levy said he had been briefed by his French counterpart on his recent talks in Paris with senior Syrian officials but was not optimistic negotiations would soon resume.
"It depends on Syria," Levy said. "We have no desire to cut Syria off from the circle of peace but Syria needs to understand that it must take the step it needs to take.
"He (de Charette) will have talks soon in the coming days in Syria. He will brief me and we'll see if there will be progress," Levy said.
Talks between Israel and Syria over the fate of the Golan Heights, captured by the Jewish state in 1967, broke off one year ago after a wave of suicide bombings in Israel.
Syria wants talks to resume at the point where they left off under Israel's previous centre-left government, which did not rule out the possibility of withdrawal from the Golan.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, elected in May, has said he wants talks with no preconditions but has insisted Israel will remain in control of the strategic heights.
